Many times. It will make it fast, cost-efficient, and secure. It will think about failure modes we c...
item.description:
作者：Guillermo Rauch 账号：@rauchg 简介：@vercel CEO
We will all be learning in coming weeks & months, that most human-made software:
▫️ Was really slow ▫️ Had many security vulnerabilities ▫️ Was under-specified and incorrect
AI will rewrite it all. Many times. It will make it fast, cost-efficient, and secure. It will think about failure modes we couldn't wrap our heads around.
It will prove, formally verify, load test, harden. It will turn memory-unsafe foundations into robust, optimized ones. If you ask, it'll thoroughly document it, teach you about it, make diagrams, animations, and slide decks.
In many ways, we are witnessing the true birth of software engineering.

item.title: The Inside Story of the 50 Who Built Modern AI With Kevin Roose
item.description:
播客：AI & I by Every
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:17 A couple years ago, you know, we had to fact check the AIs, and now the AIs fact check me. I'm playing with everything. Literally, like, I can't keep track. I have agents now that are, like, correcting my other agents. It's a huge mess.
Speaker 2 | 00:18 - 00:19 The AGI Chronicles.
Speaker 3 | 00:19 - 00:21 It was so good.
Speaker 2 | 00:21 - 00:21 Was it?
Speaker 3 | 00:21 - 00:22 It was phenomenal.
Speaker 2 | 00:22 - 00:23 Why did you like it?
Speaker 3 | 00:24 - 00:31 Like, it addresses the question that so many of us have when it comes to this moment in AI, which is just like, how did we get here?
Speaker 2 | 00:31 - 00:32 Mhmm.
Speaker 3 | 00:32 - 00:36 And it feels like the canonical answer Yeah. To that.
Speaker 2 | 00:36 - 00:44 Yeah. And Kevin, so it's by Kevin Roose, former New York Times, writer, currently the host of Machine Gods with Casey Newton.
Speaker 3 | 00:44 - 00:46 Which is also phenomenal.
Speaker 2 | 00:46 - 00:59 Friend of the pod. He's been on the show before. I think a great writer, and he was just basically inside of all the labs in the last decade watching them build AI, and this is his, like, canonical account of how that happened.
Speaker 3 | 00:59 - 01:37 It's not just the account of how it happened. It's also his experience as a journalist who was covering the 150 people who were tinkering to figure this out, and I just highly recommend it. You're gonna get a copy of it if you're at thesis with us on Thursday. And I think this is gonna be a book that's gonna have staying power, so I'm excited for it. Kevin, welcome to the pod.
Speaker 3 | 01:37 - 01:49 So excited to have you here. You are on such a role. I I hate to be interviewing you after you've been interviewed by Walter Isaacson and the like, but such an honor to have you here.
Speaker 1 | 01:50 - 01:52 Thanks so much for having me. This is a great honor for me too.
Speaker 3 | 01:53 - 01:59 And congratulations. Your book has been out for a few weeks and you are already a New York Times bestseller.
Speaker 1 | 02:00 - 02:19 Yeah. It's pretty wild. I have written books before that have not gone nearly this well. I think we got sort of lucky with everyone starting to care about AI, this fall when things started going haywire. So in a weird sense, I think the book has benefited from that attention.
Speaker 3 | 02:20 - 02:32 And you've spent more time than most people in the world with the, you know, 50 or so people that have really built AGI. Are we doomed? I don't think
Speaker 1 | 02:32 - 02:52 we're doomed. But we have a lot to do, if that makes sense. I think, you know, I... Part of why I wanted to write the book was to settle this question in my own mind, you know. Are we careening toward an existential cliff?
Speaker 1 | 02:52 - 03:37 Is it all hype? And the book doesn't, it's not really an attempt to settle that question, but I did learn a lot by interviewing the 50 people you mentioned plus like, you know, a 150 people in total who are sort of like connected to and involved in this scene. And I came away thinking both that there are some real risks ahead and some real needles that we'll need to thread as a society, but that we can do it. We have navigated hard challenges in our history. This is maybe one of the hardest, but I think we can do it and I don't think anything is set in stone or predestined.
Speaker 1 | 03:37 - 03:46 I think the choices that we make right now matter a lot in terms of how the next few years or few decades go.
Speaker 3 | 03:47 - 04:11 You had said a few years ago that you expected there to be some level of regulation after something went wrong. And, you know, we're there, right? A few things have gone wrong. We've had the hugging face incident and a number of other cybersecurity concerns. How do you see this going right?
Speaker 3 | 04:11 - 04:14 Right? Like, what needs to happen for us to course correct?
Speaker 1 | 04:16 - 04:46 Well, I think it's clear that we're not going to get federal regulation of AI, at least right now, from the Trump administration. I think what would need to happen for them to take a more active role is for something bad to happen. Right? We we saw this after nine eleven. We've seen this after disasters in our country's history where something that isn't on a lot of people's minds suddenly becomes the only thing people care about.
Speaker 1 | 04:46 - 05:31 We pass some, you know, congress passes some hastily written legislation or there's some executive action and we know how to do that. We know how to respond to a crisis. My hope is that we don't have to have a crisis for the government to respond, for regulatory bodies to respond. I think the first step would be to create some kind of industry standard, right? Some kind of certification program where in order to release your model or in order to deploy your model to the public, you have to kind of subject it to some standard safety testing to make sure it's not gonna go out there and do autonomous cyber attacks or be weaponized to create novel bioweapons.
Speaker 1 | 05:33 - 05:55 That seems like basic table stakes to me. We require pharmaceutical companies to test their drugs before selling them to the public. We should require AI companies to test their models before offering them to the public. So that's a first step. From there, I think you probably need some kind of a coordination mechanism for slowing down the frontier.
Speaker 1 | 05:55 - 06:34 I think this is something that I've been convinced of in the last couple of months. I didn't think it was going to be possible to slow down. I thought there were too many sort of forces pushing us toward acceleration, acceleration, acceleration. But I think we've seen from Dario and Demis and Sam and a lot of other AI leaders that they really do think this is moving too quickly. They really do want to buy the safety research teams at these companies some time to come up with new ways of controlling these systems and monitoring them so that we don't have, you know, more hugging face like incidents happening at a more regular cadence.
Speaker 3 | 06:35 - 07:17 And what I love about this book is that to some degree, for the majority of people that are engaging with AI, AI was something that kind of came out of nowhere for the majority of people. Right? You know, we're all going about our daily lives and then all of a sudden, this really kind of like hit the news in in sort of like a surprising and exciting way. And then ever since every few months, there are even more incred incredible, you know, advancements in the technology. But what was so cool about the book and about you writing this book in particular is that you've actually been tracking this story the whole time.
Speaker 3 | 07:17 - 07:35 You've been a tech reporter for over a decade And you were in the rooms as these companies were forming, as people were thinking of building these technologies. Can you tell me a little bit about what was the moment where you realized that you wanted to write this book?
Speaker 1 | 07:36 - 08:24 Well, the the moment I realized that I wanted to write this book came relatively late in the process. I was trying to avoid writing this book because I thought this is gonna be very hard. Someone's gonna have to go interview these 150 people and write down their stories, and I hope, that Walter Isaacson or someone of his stature wakes up one day and decides to write the book so that I don't have to do it. But that kept not happening, And I had a couple of motivations for eventually deciding to write the book, which I did, around the the sort of early twenty twenty five time period. One was, as you mentioned, I've been covering tech for more than a decade.
Speaker 1 | 08:24 - 09:03 I've known a lot of these AI researchers and people for a long time. I had written a previous book about AI that came out in 2021, but I really felt like I had actually not gotten the full s...
